title: General Sherman's thousand acres
lede: When a syndicate of Los Angeles power brokers bought most of the southern San Fernando Valley in 1909, streetcar builder Moses Sherman kept 1,000 acres for himself. In 1927 he subdivided them, selling land for about $780 an acre, and the town took his name. Half a century later a shopping mall at Ventura and Sepulveda made Sherman Oaks the capital of Valley culture.
tl: The Los Angeles Suburban Homes Company buys 47,500 acres of the southern Valley.
Moses Sherman keeps about 1,000 acres around today's Ventura and Sepulveda for himself.

The Northridge earthquake damages the Galleria, which later closes and is rebuilt as an open-air center in 2002.

p: In 1909 a syndicate that included Los Angeles Times publisher Harrison Gray Otis, his son-in-law Harry Chandler and streetcar builder Moses Sherman bought 47,500 acres of the Valley and laid out towns and boulevards. Sherman kept about 1,000 acres for himself and in 1927 subdivided them as Sherman Oaks. The street names still read like a list of the partners: Sherman Way, Chandler Boulevard and Hazeltine Avenue, named for Sherman's daughter.

The Sherman Oaks Galleria opened in 1980 on the corner where Sherman's original holdings sat, and it quickly became the center of Valley teenage life, immortalized in Fast Times at Ridgemont High in 1982. The 1994 Northridge earthquake damaged it badly, and it was rebuilt as an open-air center that reopened in 2002.
